subject: Climate & Environment
title: How the Ocean Regulates Climate
description: A quick win: understand How the Ocean Regulates Climate.

hook.text: The ocean has absorbed over 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases since 1970.

buildup.text: Water holds 1,000 times more heat than air. The ocean is Earth's giant thermal battery.

discovery.text: Without the ocean absorbing that heat, the atmosphere would already be far hotter.

twist.text: But the ocean is reaching its limits. Surface waters are warming faster than ever recorded.

climax.text: Warmer oceans fuel stronger storms, bleach corals, and raise sea levels as water expands.

punchline.text: The ocean hid most of the warming. Now it's sending it back.

quiz.question: What percentage of extra heat has the ocean absorbed since 1970?

details.summary: The ocean absorbs roughly 90 percent of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases and about a quarter of human-produced carbon dioxide. Through evaporation, currents, and gas exchange it redistributes energy across the planet, moderating temperatures on land.
details.whyItMatters: Without the ocean's heat and carbon buffering, average global temperatures would be far higher. Understanding this role is key to climate projections.
takeaways: The ocean absorbs about 90 percent of excess planetary heat
It also takes up roughly 25 percent of human CO2 emissions
Evaporation and currents redistribute energy worldwide

faq.question: How does the ocean absorb carbon dioxide?
faq.answer: CO2 dissolves into surface water through gas exchange with the atmosphere. Cold, dense water sinks and carries dissolved carbon to the deep ocean, a process called the solubility pump. Marine organisms also fix carbon through photosynthesis.

faq.question: Could the ocean stop absorbing heat and carbon?
faq.answer: Warmer water holds less dissolved gas, and a more stratified ocean mixes less efficiently. Scientists worry that continued warming could weaken the ocean's capacity as a carbon and heat sink, accelerating atmospheric warming.
